purpose: Propranolol is used to treat high blood pressure, certain heart rhythm problems, chest pain (angina), and heart failure. It is also used to prevent migraines, reduce symptoms of anxiety (like a racing heart before a big event), and treat a thyroid condition called hyperthyroidism. Some people take it to help prevent a second heart attack.
how_it_works: Your heart has special receptors that respond to adrenaline, which can make your heart beat faster and harder. Propranolol blocks those receptors, so your heart beats more slowly and with less force. This helps lower your blood pressure, steady your heart rhythm, and reduce the workload on your heart.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired or fatigued, cold hands and feet, dizziness or lightheadedness, slow heartbeat, upset stomach, nausea, and sometimes trouble sleeping or unusual dreams. Some people notice reduced sex drive or mild depression.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medication suddenly without talking to your doctor — stopping too quickly can cause serious heart problems. Tell your doctor if you have asthma or breathing problems, since propranolol can make breathing harder. It can also mask the signs of low blood sugar if you are diabetic, so check your blood sugar closely. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can increase dizziness. Let your doctor know about all other medications you take, as many can interact with propranolol.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on what condition is being treated. For high blood pressure, a common starting dose is 40 mg taken twice a day, which may be adjusted up to 160–320 mg per day. For anxiety or migraines, lower doses are often used. Extended-release (long-acting) versions are taken once a day. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes and try to take it at the same time each day.
